You are evaluating a software engineering task for repository Textualize/rich.

Problem Statement:
Strip problematic private escape sequences

## Type of changes

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Documentation / docstrings
- [ ] Tests
- [ ] Other

## Checklist

- [x] I've run the latest [black](https://github.com/psf/black) with default args on new code.
- [x] I've updated CHANGELOG.md and CONTRIBUTORS.md where appropriate.
- [x] I've added tests for new code.
- [x] I accept that @willmcgugan may be pedantic in the code review.

## Description

["Private escape sequences"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Fp_Escape_sequences) are escape sequences that are reserved for private use, though `\x1b7` and `\x1b8` are commonly used for storing and restoring the current cursor position. When those escape codes are not stripped the cursor jumps around and causes Rich to write garbage output. An example of a program that uses this cursor store/restore functionality is the APK package manager in Alpine Linux:

https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/apk-tools/-/blob/48d91f482eb48a0a107b714ee183bb7e07782e14/src/print.c#L232-240

This commit updates the ANSI parser to ignore the `\x1b0`-`\x1b?` escape sequences, thus preventing them from being printed and causing havoc.

steps.message:
The issue describes a problem where "private escape sequences" (specifically `\x1b0` through `\x1b?`) are not being stripped by the ANSI parser, leading to garbage output in some environments.

In `rich/ansi.py`, the `re_ansi` regular expression is used to tokenize ANSI escape sequences. The second part of the regex handles the CSI (Control Sequence Introducer) and other escape sequences:
`r"(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))"`

The group `[@-Z\\\\-_]` matches characters in the range `@` to `Z`, `\`, `-`, and `_`. 
The characters `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` are not matched by this character class. 
Specifically, the ASCII characters from `0` (48) to `?` (63) are:
`0123456789:;<=>?`
These are all before `@` (64) in the ASCII table.

To strip these, we need to expand the character range in `re_ansi` to include `0` through `?`.

FILES: rich/ansi.py:12-14
ROOT CAUSE: The ANSI regular expression `re_ansi` does not include the character range `0-?` in its match for single-character escape sequences, allowing `\x1b0` through `\x1b?` to pass through.
CHANGE: Update the character class `[@-Z\\\\-_]` to `[0-Z\\\\-_]` (or explicitly `[0-?@-Z\\\\-_]`).
TEST: Add a test case to `tests/test_ansi.py` that includes `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` sequences and verify they are stripped.

Wait, let me double check the ASCII range.
`0` is 48.
`?` is 63.
`@` is 64.
So `0-?` is the range we need.

The current regex is:
`r"(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))"`

Proposed change:
`r"(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))"` -> `r"(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))"`
No, I should change `[@-Z\\\\-_]` to `[0-Z\\\\-_]`.
Actually, `0-?` are the characters from 48 to 63.
The range `0-Z` would cover 48 (`0`) to 90 (`Z`).
`@` is 64.
So `[0-Z]` covers `0-?` and `@-Z`.

Current: `[@-Z\\\\-_]`
Target: `[0-Z\\\\-_]`

Let's verify the test file. `tests/test_ansi.py` has `test_decode_issue_2688` which tests stripping. I'll add a similar test case for private escape sequences.

TEST: `pytest tests/test_ansi.py`
